overview: Imagine a government that could move with its herds, argue through family alliances, send huge embassies on horseback and stretch influence across the Volga to Ural steppe. That was the sixteenth-century Nogai Horde at its strongest. Yet the atlas keeps one Nogai label from 1530 to 1783, long after civil war, famine, Muscovite conquest and Kalmyk pressure scattered its political center. Great Nogai, Lesser Nogai, Altıoğul, Budjak, Yedisan, Yedichkul, Dzhambuiluk and Kuban communities followed different leaders and bargained with Russia, Crimea, the Ottomans and neighboring steppe powers. Their world joined mobile pastoral skill to markets, grain growing, books, diplomacy, warfare and painful captive trading. This card follows those branching histories, then enters homes, work, food, learning, health, water and play, marking later ethnography when early sources fall silent. Russia's 1783 annexation of Crimea explains the atlas ending; it did not erase Nogai people, language or memory.

periods.title: Edige's Manghits and a new political inheritance
periods.summary: Edige and his descendants led Manghit communities inside the changing Jochid world. Their authority did not make them Chinggisid khans, so leadership grew through office, descent, alliance and control of mobile groups.

periods.title: A Nogai confederation between Volga and Yaik
periods.summary: Under Musa and his relatives, the Manghit yurt became a strong independent confederation. Saraychik, river crossings, seasonal pastures and influence over neighboring thrones mattered more than a hard border line.

periods.title: Power, factions and the atlas's broadest footprint
periods.summary: Yusuf and Ismail headed rival networks while Nogai leaders negotiated with Moscow, Crimea, Kazan and Astrakhan. The atlas begins during real Nogai power, but its two polygons already mix incompatible geography and labeling.

periods.title: Great, Lesser and Altıoğul paths diverge
periods.summary: Muscovy's conquest of Astrakhan, civil war and famine weakened the lower-Volga center. Great Nogai remained east of the Volga; Lesser Nogai moved toward Azov and Kuban; Altıoğul groups ranged around Emba.

periods.title: Kalmyk pressure and a Nogai world from Caspian to Danube
periods.summary: Kalmyk attacks accelerated movement toward the Caucasus and Black Sea. Evliya encountered named Nogai groups around Budjak, Azov, Kuban, Circassia and the lower Volga, under several overlapping powers.

periods.title: Yedisan, Yedichkul, Dzhambuiluk, Bilhorod and Kuban
periods.summary: The eighteenth-century map was a mosaic of Nogai hordes tied in different ways to Crimean khans and Ottoman officials. Their herds, migrations and armies remained important even without a single Nogai capital.

periods.title: Russian protectorate, competing oaths and annexation
periods.summary: After Küçük Kaynarca, Russian commanders sought Nogai allegiance while leaders shifted sides, resisted and negotiated. Russia annexed Crimea in 1783; that explains the atlas endpoint better than the fall of one still-unified Nogai Horde.

sections.title: Read the atlas as evidence about the atlas

items.text: The exact id is nogai-horde, labeled “Nogai Horde” and indexed circa 1530 to 1783. The index supplies no alias, historical link or author-written summary. The coverage register calls it a state and records five border intervals, but those database fields do not prove one government lasted unchanged for 253 years.

At 1492 the exact id is absent. Tested Astrakhan and lower-Volga places sit in a broad golden-horde polygon; Emba, Aktobe, Mangyshlak and Orenburg sit in white-horde; Kuban, Azov and Crimea sit in an Ottoman feature labeled Crimean Khanate. This predecessor seam is already a rough editorial patchwork.

The 1530 layer contains two separate nogai-horde Polygons. The larger, unlabeled one has 99 positions and spans roughly 28.09° to 61.00° east, 44.44° to 58.21° north. It includes tested Astrakhan, lower Volga, Atyrau, Yaik, Emba, Aktobe, Orenburg and even Kazan, an enormous locator rather than a defensible frontier.

The other 1530 polygon has 92 positions, spans roughly 37.47° to 48.22° east and 41.20° to 46.81° north, and covers tested Kizlyar, Terek, Stavropol, Cherkessk and Kuban. Its embedded label says “Astrakhan Khanate,” yet Astrakhan itself lies outside it. That is an explicit id-label-geometry collision.

From 1600 through 1783 the target shrinks to one 33-position polygon around tested Atyrau, Emba and Aktobe. Lower-Volga and western Nogai worlds disappear from the id. At 1783 the polygon vanishes into Russian, Ottoman and generic Central Asian features. The redraw cannot be read as a complete migration diary.

sections.title: A horde that was a political network, not a blob

items.text: Nogai political leadership grew from Edige's Manghit descendants. Because they were not Chinggisids, a biy could lead the confederation but could not simply claim the khan's sacred dynastic rank. Offices, councils, wing leadership and relationships with Chinggisid princes turned a family network into government without copying a European crown.

Nogai leaders drew legitimacy from Manghit tribal custom and descent from Edige. Crimean khans answered with Chinggisid töre, while Ottoman sultans stressed Islamic sovereignty. The result was not a tidy ladder: the same leader might bargain with Moscow, serve a Crimean khan on campaign and still defend his own ulus's right to move.

The terms Great Nogai and Lesser Nogai describe branches formed during dispersal, not two halves cut neatly by a ruler. Great Nogai remained mainly east of the Volga under growing Moscow pressure; Lesser Nogai gathered around Azov and Kuban in the Crimean sphere. Altıoğul groups followed another route near Emba.

Internal names multiplied because people followed leaders, kin and pasture opportunities. Ulu, Kiçi, Urumbet, Şıdak, Mansurlu, Çobaneli, Nevruzeli and Deveyli were among groups recorded in the seventeenth century. A modern viewer should imagine overlapping camps and allegiances, not colored provinces with border posts at every edge.

Some Nogai nobles entered Muscovite service and founded durable elite lines, including families later known as Yusupov and Urusov. Their careers, marriages and estates show one kind of continuity: political incorporation could transform status while preserving genealogy. It did not mean every ordinary herding household shared an aristocrat's choices or rewards.

sections.title: Power, famine and splintering in the sixteenth century

items.text: Musa's turn-of-the-sixteenth-century confederation reached from the lower Volga and Yaik toward western Kazakhstan and influenced Astrakhan, Kazan and Kazakh politics. Saraychik was a capital and caravan place, but mobile rulers governed through people, pasture routes and negotiated submission. Calling the polity borderless would be wrong; drawing it like a fenced farm would also be wrong.

Muscovy conquered Kazan in 1552 and Astrakhan in 1556, planting its power on the Volga corridor that Nogai diplomacy and trade depended upon. Ismail cooperated with Ivan IV against rivals, yet Russian officials, Cossacks and neighboring leaders continually altered the bargain. “Ally,” “subject” and “enemy” could change faster than a herd changed pasture.

In the later 1550s civil war, ruined routes, flood, severe winter and long famine killed livestock and people and drove communities outward. Requests for seed, grain and relief survive in diplomacy. This crisis helps explain political dispersal much better than a story in which one decisive battle suddenly shattered a perfectly united state.

Lesser Nogai emerged around Azov and Kuban under leaders who entered the Crimean sphere, while groups reaching Budjak could fall more directly under Ottoman authority. Those migrations did not erase autonomy: Nogai mirzas continued to argue from tribal custom, choose patrons and sometimes raid the very partners who claimed to command them.

The atlas's long end date hides this central fact: by the early seventeenth century there was no single polity matching its surviving eastern polygon. Great Nogai, Lesser Nogai, Altıoğul and other communities had different leaders and neighbors. The card therefore tracks a Nogai political world after the original horde's unity had broken.

sections.title: Between Kalmyks, Crimea, the Ottomans and the steppe

items.text: Oirat groups called Kalmyks pushed west in the early seventeenth century and struck Great Nogai communities hard in the 1630s. Some Nogais submitted, some fought, and many moved toward the North Caucasus or Black Sea. Migration was a strategy of survival, but every route also placed families inside new political and ecological negotiations.

Evliya Çelebi's later travels found Nogai groups from the Danube and Budjak through Azov and Kuban to Circassia and the lower Volga. His dramatic descriptions require criticism, yet the broad pattern matches other observers: Nogai life had become a transregional network after Kalmyk pressure, not a single camp east of Astrakhan.

Crimean khans expected Nogai cavalry on campaigns and claimed the authority of Chinggisid descent. Ottoman officials also relocated groups, negotiated directly with mirzas and sometimes disciplined khans who acted without permission. Nogai communities could therefore be Crimean vassals, Ottoman dependents and active political bargainers at the same time.

Sixteenth-century heroes such as Qazi and Karasai entered later Nogai epic traditions alongside memories of struggles involving Crimea, Russia, the Ottomans and Safavids. Oral poetry preserves political meaning, not a stenographic transcript. Historians compare variants and documents before using a heroic song to reconstruct a particular march or speech.

In the Pontic steppe Nogai hordes, Crimean rulers, Cossacks, Polish-Lithuanian authorities, Ottoman officers and Russia shared and contested the same grasslands and river corridors. Later Russian settlement did not enter empty land. It reordered an inhabited frontier whose residents already traded, fought, moved and claimed routes in different ways.

sections.title: The 1770s ending was conquest, negotiation and movement

items.text: During the Russo-Ottoman war of 1768 to 1774, Nogai leaders became essential to both sides. Some allied with Russia, others stayed with Crimean or Ottoman patrons, and allegiances shifted as armies moved. Russian commanders used oaths, gifts and steppe diplomatic habits; calling every oath permanent loyalty would misread the bargaining world that produced it.

The 1774 Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca declared the Crimean Khanate independent of Ottoman authority but left it under powerful Russian influence. Nogai hordes did not become one independent nation in the process. They faced rival khans, resettlement schemes, military pressure and new demands to fit imperial categories designed elsewhere.

Russia annexed Crimea in 1783, making that year a logical atlas cutoff for the Crimean political system that encompassed many western Nogais. It is not the death date of all Nogai organization. Budjak remained Ottoman, Trans-Kuban resistance continued, and eastern Nogai communities followed histories the Crimea-centered endpoint cannot contain.

After annexation, Giray and Nogai resistance continued from Budjak and Trans-Kuban centers into the nineteenth century. The atlas transfer to a Russian polygon therefore records an imperial claim and major military change, not instant consent. People could cross a cartographic seam while still fighting the government whose color had appeared beneath them.

Later displacement carried Crimean and Nogai Tatars into Ottoman Anatolia and the Balkans, while other Nogai communities remained in the North Caucasus, lower Volga and steppe. Today Nogai language and identity continue in several Russian regions and diasporas. A state ended; a people, language and memory did not.

sections.title: Herds, markets, raids and the work of moving

items.text: Seasonal pastoralism organized much of sixteenth-century life. One major cycle linked winter grounds near the lower Syr Darya with summer pastures by the Yaik; another linked lower-Volga winters with northern summer grounds. Routes belonged to communities and mirzas, and redistributing pasture could produce political quarrels as serious as arguments over titles.

Sheep, horses, cattle and camels supplied milk, meat, hides, felt, transport and exchange value. Winter cold, deep snow and livestock disease could destroy wealth quickly, because a herd was also pantry, wardrobe and vehicle fleet. The 1550s disaster was therefore not merely “bad business”; it attacked the machinery of daily survival.

Nogai embassies were also enormous logistical events. A 1556 report counted a mission and trading party with hundreds of people, thousands of horses and sheep; records track feed, lodging, safe conduct and market access. Such numbers are claims recorded by officials, not a census, but they reveal diplomacy traveling on hooves.

Seventeenth-century Nogai economies also included grain. Evliya reported Çobaneli and Budjak groups using two-humped camels to pull plows and carts and sowing wheat, barley and millet. That evidence punctures the cartoon of people who only followed animals; mobile herding and cultivation could work together in one regional economy.

Trade and raiding both moved wealth. Nogais supplied livestock products and horses, taxed or protected routes, and sold captives; they were also captured and sold by enemies. A child-readable history must say plainly that slavery harmed real people. It was an economic institution, not a colorful adventure attached to fast cavalry.

sections.title: Families, rank and childhood, what we can and cannot see

items.text: Diplomatic books constantly name brothers, sons, nephews, wives, daughters and foster kin because households linked politics. Ismail tried to bind younger relatives to his agreements, while rival branches moved with women and children. Elite family evidence is vivid, but it cannot tell us the average household size or everyone's private feelings.

Later Nogai ethnography describes households ordered by age and gender, marriage payments, parental negotiation and strong obligations among relatives. It also records women's work and authority inside families. Because those observations come from the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, the card treats them as possible continuity, never as a sixteenth-century household census.

Children learned the skills a moving household needed: tending animals, handling materials, recognizing kin obligations and listening to stories. That is a cautious reconstruction from the pastoral economy and later childrearing record. The sources do not give a Nogai child's hour-by-hour timetable, age at first riding or a universal division of chores.

Women's lives varied sharply by wealth, age, marital status, captivity and location. A mirza's marriage could make an alliance; an enslaved woman had radically less freedom; ordinary pastoral work demanded knowledge and endurance. Later family research helps name domestic roles, but it cannot turn all women across three centuries into one character.

Rank mattered. Biys and mirzas commanded followers and large herds; religious specialists and envoys carried knowledge; ordinary ulus members bore much of the herding and moving; captives faced coercion. Mobility offered communities political choices, yet poverty or violence could strip that choice away. “Nomad” was never a single social class.

sections.title: Learning, belief and a letter whose original is missing

items.text: Nogai Muslim learning was real even though schools are poorly mapped. A 1550 letter mentions a foster brother who went to Crimea to learn writing. Another request sought the poet and interpreter Muhammad Yar. These are named cases of mobile education and court literacy, not proof that every camp had a classroom.

Nogai leaders cited the Qur'an, the Gospels and the words of learned men in diplomacy. In 1538 a biy requested paper, saffron and six colors, evidence consistent with book production. Learned advisers, mullahs and interpreters connected oral politics to written Islamic and chancery worlds across the steppe.

Evliya identified Nogais as Muslims and described a Nogai scholar who became a Qur'an commentator and hadith expert within Ottoman society. He also assigned legal schools rather too neatly to many groups. His testimony proves learned careers existed; it does not establish the exact beliefs or religious practice of every household.

The safest short written sample is an archival form: “Исмаиль мирза белому князю поклон.” Transliteration: “Ismail' mirza belomu knyazyu poklon.” Translation: “Ismail Mirza sends a bow, or greeting, to the White Prince.” It appears in a letter delivered in July 1551 and copied into Muscovite embassy books.

That sample is Early Modern Russian chancery language, not a surviving Nogai autograph. Muscovite scribes recorded a translated diplomatic message; the lost incoming document may have used a Turkic written register. Labeling the copied language honestly is better history than manufacturing Arabic-script Nogai words that no checked contemporary manuscript preserves.

Later ethnography records two Nogai portable felt-home forms: a collapsible lattice-framed terme and a smaller otav that could be carried whole. Wooden frames, felt covers, roof openings and central hearths made houses movable and repairable. This helps explain pastoral logistics, but the detailed description is later evidence, not a photograph of 1551.

Felt turned sheep's wool into walls, rugs, bags, straps, footwear and outer clothing. Household production demanded sorting, wetting, rolling and smoothing wool, with different quality for different uses. A portable house was therefore a craft project as well as shelter; its walls began as many hours of skilled work.

Clothing visible in seventeenth-century testimony included sheepskin coats, lambskin caps, colored cloth garments, belts, boots and riding gear. Dress varied with wealth, trade and regional neighbors. The funny-looking part to a modern child may be packing your wall and wardrobe from the same flock; the historical point is material efficiency.

Evliya listed millet bread and gruel, dried dairy foods, soups, horse meat and boza among Nogai foods, while later food studies document a broad dairy-and-meat repertoire plus grains and preserved products. His claim that people never drank water is rhetorical exaggeration, especially beside records of drought and desperate well digging.

Meals changed by season, herd health, market access, wealth and region. Dairy could be processed when animals were milking; meat and grain could be stored or traded; famine wrecked every plan. No source supports one universal daily menu. “Nogai food” names a repertoire, not a lunchbox issued to everyone for 253 years.

sections.title: Health, water, toilets, games and honest blank spaces

items.text: Sixteenth-century sources document hunger, exposure, drowning, wounds, illness and livestock disease far more often than treatment. The great famine brought malnutrition and death; an ill biy appears in correspondence, but no clinical notes survive. We can discuss health risks securely without inventing a Nogai pharmacy or claiming an unrecorded cure worked.

Later Nogai ethnography records respected healers, practical remedies, ritual treatment and veterinary knowledge, plus sayings linking cleanliness and health. Those traditions may preserve older elements, but their recorded nineteenth- and twentieth-century form cannot simply be dated to 1530. The card separates continuity evidence from contemporary proof.

Water followed rivers, seasonal camps, wells and weather. In the 1550s drought, one account says people dug deeply and still found little; a flood then ruined Saraychik fields. These crises show why route knowledge mattered. They do not prove ordinary water quality, who fetched it or a standard treatment before drinking.

The checked sixteenth- and seventeenth-century sources do not securely describe a Nogai camp toilet, latrine, sewer or waste-disposal rule. Later dwelling and medicine studies also focus elsewhere. The honest answer to “where did people poop?” is that people certainly did, but this evidence set cannot document the arrangement without guessing.

Recorded modern Nogai childlore includes counting-out, drawing lots, game choruses, teasing, jokes, tongue twisters and song appeals. Collected Edige epics add heroic performance and memory. Both repertoires changed through transmission, so neither source tells us exactly what a child heard or shouted beside the Yaik in 1600.

ending.text: The 1783 endpoint is an atlas handoff tied to Russia's annexation of Crimea and expanding claims across the steppe. No single Nogai Horde had survived intact until that date. Nogai resistance, migration and community life continued in Budjak, Trans-Kuban, the North Caucasus, lower Volga, Ottoman lands and elsewhere.
